claim: Grid firing fields have been proposed as a neural substrate for spatial localisation in general or for path integration in particular.
source: Grid firing fields have been proposed as a neural substrate for spatial localisation in general or for path integration in particular.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: Grid firing can either be anchored to the task environment, or can encode distance travelled independently of the task reference frame.
source: We find that grid firing can either be anchored to the task environment, or can encode distance travelled independently of the task reference frame.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Anchoring of grid cells varied between and within sessions.
source: Anchoring varied between and within sessions, while spatial firing of non-grid cells was either coherent with the grid population, or was stably anchored to the task environment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and data analysis.

claim: Spatial firing of non-grid cells was either coherent with the grid population, or was stably anchored to the task environment.
source: Anchoring varied between and within sessions, while spatial firing of non-grid cells was either coherent with the grid population, or was stably anchored to the task environment.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of non-grid cell activity.

claim: When reward location is indicated by a visual cue, performance is similar regardless of whether grid cells are task-anchored or not.
source: We find that when reward location is indicated by a visual cue, performance is similar regardless of whether grid cells are task-anchored or not, arguing against a role for grid representations when location cues are available.
evidence: This is a key finding from behavioral performance data.

claim: In the absence of the visual cue, performance was enhanced when grid cells were anchored to the task environment.
source: By contrast, in the absence of the visual cue, performance was enhanced when grid cells were anchored to the task environment.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral performance data comparing task-anchored and task-independent conditions.

claim: Anchoring of grid cells to task reference frames selectively enhances performance when path integration is required.
source: Our results suggest that anchoring of grid cells to task reference frames selectively enhances performance when path integration is required.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Grid representations generated by neurons in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) are thought to be critical for spatial behaviours and other cognitive functions that require structured representations.
source: Grid representations generated by neurons in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) are thought to be critical for spatial behaviours and other cognitive functions that require structured representations (Moser et al., 2008; Whittington et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The range of behaviours to which grid cells contribute is unclear.
source: However, the range of behaviours to which grid cells contribute is unclear (Ginosar et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation indicating ongoing debate in the field.

claim: Grid cell populations can generate high capacity codes.
source: On the one hand, theoretical arguments that grid cell populations can generate high capacity codes imply that they could in principle contribute to all spatial behaviours (Fiete et al., 2008; Mathis et al., 2012; Sreenivasan and Fiete, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Grid cells are hypothesised to generate position representations by integrating self-motion signals.
source: On the other hand, if the behavioural importance of grid cells follows from their hypothesised ability to generate position representations by integrating self-motion signals (McNaughton et al., 2006), then their behavioural roles may be restricted to tasks that involve path integration strategies.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a hypothesis in the literature.

claim: Lesions of the MEC disrupt place representations in the hippocampus and impair performance in spatial memory tasks.
source: Lesions of the MEC disrupt place representations in the hippocampus and impair performance in spatial memory tasks (Brun et al., 2008; Hales et al., 2021; Hales et al., 2018; Hales et al., 2014; Miao et al., 2015; Schlesiger et al., 2015; Steffenach et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: MEC lesion impairments are often incomplete in that hippocampal place representations remain, although they are less stable, and some spatial tasks can still be solved.
source: These impairments are often incomplete in that hippocampal place representations remain, although they are less stable, and some spatial tasks can still be solved.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited experimental studies.

claim: Deletion during postnatal development of NMDA receptors from neurons in the MEC and nearby structures reduces the number of detected grid cells in these areas while having less effect on other spatial cell types.
source: Deletion during postnatal development of NMDA receptors from neurons in the MEC and nearby structures reduces the number of detected grid cells in these areas while having less effect on other spatial cell types (Gil et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: NMDA receptor deletion in MEC impairs path integration without affecting other spatial behaviours.
source: This manipulation impairs path integration without affecting other spatial behaviours (Gil et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: Targeted inactivation of stellate cells in layer 2 of the MEC impairs learning of both path integration-dependent behaviours and cue-based navigation more generally.
source: In contrast, targeted inactivation of stellate cells in layer 2 of the MEC, which are thought to be a major grid cell population (Gu et al., 2018; Rowland et al., 2018), impairs learning of both path integration-dependent behaviours and cue-based navigation more generally (Qin et al., 2018; Tennant et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Stellate cells in layer 2 of the MEC are thought to be a major grid cell population.
source: In contrast, targeted inactivation of stellate cells in layer 2 of the MEC, which are thought to be a major grid cell population (Gu et al., 2018; Rowland et al., 2018), impairs learning of both path integration-dependent behaviours and cue-based navigation more generally (Qin et al., 2018; Tennant et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: For MEC manipulations it is difficult to establish whether impairments result from deficits in grid firing per se, or from other alterations in the circuit and its potential for plasticity.
source: However, for all of these manipulations it is difficult to establish whether impairments result from deficits in grid firing per se, or from other alterations in the circuit and its potential for plasticity.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of perturbation experiments.

claim: It is unclear whether functions that appear resistant to perturbations of the MEC could have been restored by adaptive compensatory changes.
source: It is also unclear whether functions that in these experiments appear resistant to perturbations of the MEC could have been restored by adaptive compensatory changes.
evidence: This is speculation about potential confounds in perturbation experiments.

claim: Hypothesised functions for neural codes can be corroborated by correlations with behavioural outcomes, while dissociations between representations and behaviour may rule out hypothesised roles for a given code.
source: Thus, hypothesised functions for neural codes can be corroborated by correlations with behavioural outcomes, while dissociations between representations and behaviour may rule out hypothesised roles for a given code.
evidence: This is a methodological principle based on scientific reasoning.

claim: The idea that grid codes provide a general-purpose spatial code predicts that they are always available and are stably anchored to the external environment.
source: In the case of grid codes, the idea that they provide a general-purpose spatial code predicts that they are always available and are stably anchored to the external environment (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: In circular track environments, grid firing patterns are maintained but are no longer anchored to the environment.
source: This notion is challenged by observations that in circular track environments, grid firing patterns are maintained but are no longer anchored to the environment (Jacob et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: In circular tracks, grid representations are informative about distance travelled but not about absolute position.
source: In this case, the grid representations are informative about distance travelled but not about absolute position (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an inference from cited work and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Spatial representations within populations of MEC neurons that include grid cells can be unstable with the network spontaneously remapping between different representations of location.
source: Spatial representations within populations of MEC neurons that include grid cells can also be unstable with the network spontaneously remapping between different representations of location (Low et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: It is unclear whether instability of grid representations impacts performance of spatial tasks.
source: Thus, it appears that grid representations are not necessarily stably anchored to the external world, but it is unclear whether this instability impacts performance of spatial tasks.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: 103 out of 1881 neurons were identified as grid cells (11.4±17.4 grid cells/mouse, range 0.4–9.5%).
source: By comparing the hexagonal symmetry of spatial autocorrelograms of neural activity in the open arena with corresponding shuffled data, we identified 103/1881 neurons as grid cells (11.4±17.4 grid cells/mouse, range 0.4–9.5%, Supplementary file 1) (see Materials and methods for classification procedures).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: Grid cells had field sizes of 7.5±3.3 cm and grid spacing of 72.5±13.7 cm.
source: These grid cells had field sizes of 7.5±3.3 cm and grid spacing of 72.5±13.7 cm and were found in dorsomedial parts of the MEC.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental measurements.

claim: Grid cells were found in dorsomedial parts of the MEC.
source: These grid cells had field sizes of 7.5±3.3 cm and grid spacing of 72.5±13.7 cm and were found in dorsomedial parts of the MEC.
evidence: This is a direct report of anatomical localization from experimental data.

claim: 68 of 103 grid cells had peaks in their periodograms within 5% of an integer multiple of the spatial frequency of the track repetition, consistent with task-anchored firing.
source: We found that 68 of 103 grid cells had peaks in their periodograms within 5% of an integer multiple of the spatial frequency of the track repetition, consistent with their activity being anchored to the reference frame provided by the virtual track (Figure 2A and D–E).
evidence: This is a direct report of data analysis results shown in Figure 2.

claim: 32 of 103 grid cells had periodograms with peaks at frequencies outside 5% of an integer multiple of the track length, indicating task-independent activity.
source: By contrast, 32 of 103 grid cells had periodograms with peaks at frequencies outside 5% of an integer multiple of the track length, indicating that their activity was not coupled to the task reference frame (Figure 2B and D–E).
evidence: This is a direct report of data analysis results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Grid cells with periodograms lacking peaks above the false alarm threshold (aperiodic grid cells) were rare (3/103).
source: Grid cells with periodograms lacking peaks above the false alarm threshold, which we will refer to as aperiodic grid cells, were rare (3/103) (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is a direct report of data analysis results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Among non-grid cells, the proportion of neurons with task-anchored firing was similar to grid cells, but task-independent periodic firing was rarer, while aperiodic firing neurons were more common.
source: When we carried out similar analyses for non-grid cells, we found that the proportion of neurons with task-anchored firing was similar, but task-independent periodic firing was rarer, while aperiodic firing neurons were more common (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a direct report of data analysis comparing grid and non-grid cells shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Task-anchored grid cells showed clear firing rate peaks associated with specific track locations.
source: Consistent with their classification, task-anchored grid cells showed clear firing rate peaks associated with specific track locations (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Task-independent and aperiodic grid cells lacked clear firing rate peaks.
source: By contrast, task-independent and aperiodic grid cells lacked clear firing rate peaks (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Grid cells with session-level task-anchored firing had substantially higher spatial information scores compared with task-independent firing.
source: These differences manifest as substantially higher spatial information scores, but similar average firing rates, for grid cells with session-level task-anchored firing compared with task-independent firing (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Grid cells with session-level task-anchored firing had similar average firing rates compared with task-independent firing.
source: These differences manifest as substantially higher spatial information scores, but similar average firing rates, for grid cells with session-level task-anchored firing compared with task-independent firing (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Features of the periodogram such as peak power and peak width did not differ between task-anchored grid cells and task-independent grid cells.
source: Features of the periodogram such as peak power and peak width did not differ between task-anchored grid cells and task-independent grid cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Aperiodic grid cells had much lower mean firing rates than task-anchored or task-independent grid cells.
source: The aperiodic grid cells had much lower mean firing rates than the task-anchored grid or task-independent grid cells suggesting that their apparent lack of periodicity reflects inactivity (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: For many grid cells there appeared to be clear changes in anchoring within a session.
source: However, for many grid cells there appeared to be clear changes in anchoring within a session (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by visual inspection of data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Switches in grid cell mode could not be explained by variation between trials in the availability of cues or rewards.
source: These switches could not be explained by variation between trials in the availability of cues or rewards, as these were interleaved in blocks that repeated throughout a session (see Materials and methods), whereas periods in which grid cell activity was in a given mode extended across the repeating blocks (e.g. Figures 3D, E—5E, F).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental design and observed data patterns.

claim: For 26.2% of grid cells (27/103) the classification was consistently (>85% of trials) task-anchored or task-independent.
source: For 26.2% of grid cells (27/103) the classification was consistently (>85% of trials) task-anchored or task-independent (Figure 3F), whereas for 73.8% of grid cells (76/103) no single coding scheme accounted for more than 85% of trials (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a direct report of data analysis results shown in Figure 3F.

claim: For 73.8% of grid cells (76/103) no single coding scheme accounted for more than 85% of trials.
source: For 26.2% of grid cells (27/103) the classification was consistently (>85% of trials) task-anchored or task-independent (Figure 3F), whereas for 73.8% of grid cells (76/103) no single coding scheme accounted for more than 85% of trials (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a direct report of data analysis results shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Spatially localised firing rate fields were present during task-anchored firing but were reduced or abolished when firing was task-independent.
source: Consistent with the classification scheme correctly separating task-anchored from task-independent activity, spatially localised firing rate fields were present during task-anchored firing but were reduced or abolished when firing was task-independent (e.g. see rate maps, Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by visual inspection of data in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Task-independent firing was associated with substantially lower spatial information scores compared to task-anchored firing, while mean firing rates were similar.
source: This difference was associated with substantially lower spatial information scores for trials with task-independent firing, while mean firing rates were similar (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Among all grid cells periods of task-anchored or task-independent firing extended in blocks across multiple trials, with the distribution of block lengths substantially different to that generated by shuffled data.
source: By contrast, among all grid cells periods of task-anchored or task-independent firing extended in blocks across multiple trials, with the distribution of block lengths substantially different to that generated by shuffled data (Figure 3—figure supplement 6)(p=0.0003, KS=0.066; DF=1765, 2359; Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison to shuffled data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Variation between grid cells in their firing mode could not be explained by the relative proportion of cued trials in a session.
source: Variation between grid cells in their firing mode also could not be explained by the relative proportion of cued trials in a session (Figure 3—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claim: Grid cells typically transitioned between task-anchored and task-independent firing modes at the same time.
source: Grid cells typically transitioned between task-anchored and task-independent firing modes at the same time (e.g. see Figure 4A–C and Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4A-C and 5E-F.

claim: Session-long agreement scores for pairs of grid cells showed strong agreement in their firing modes.
source: This manifested as strong agreement between grid cells in their session-long order of task-anchored and task-independent epochs (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: Some non-grid cells transitioned between task-anchored and task-independent modes at the same time as simultaneously recorded grid cells, whereas others remained stably anchored throughout the recording session.
source: Some non-grid cells transitioned between task-anchored and task-independent modes at the same time as simultaneously recorded grid cells, whereas others remained stably anchored throughout the recording session (Figure 4A–C and Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4A-C and 5E-F.

claim: Session-long agreement scores for pairs of grid and non-grid cells were more variable and on average lower than for pairs of grid cells.
source: As a result, session-long agreement scores for pairs of grid and non-grid cells were more variable and on average lower than for pairs of grid cells (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: Non-grid cells maintained similar spatial information between trials when grid cells were task-anchored versus when they were task-independent, whereas for grid cells task independence was associated with reduced spatial information.
source: Non-grid cells also differed from the grid cell population in that their activity maintained similar spatial information between trials when grid cells were task-anchored versus when they were task-independent, whereas for grid cells task independence was associated with reduced spatial information (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Grid cells can switch between task-anchored and task-independent firing modes within a behavioural session.
source: Together, these data indicate that grid cells can switch between task-anchored and task-independent firing modes within a behavioural session.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Switching between firing modes happens coherently across grid cell populations, which is consistent with grid cells forming networks with continuous attractor dynamics.
source: This switching happens coherently across grid cell populations, which is consistent with grid cells forming networks with continuous attractor dynamics (Barry et al., 2007; Gardner et al., 2022; Waaga et al., 2021; Yoon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from the data supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Non-grid cells within the MEC form multiple populations, with some having activity that is coherent with the grid cell network, whereas others maintain stable spatial representations independently from grid cells.
source: Our data also suggest that non-grid cells within the MEC form multiple populations, with some having activity that is coherent with the grid cell network, whereas others do not show task-independent periodic firing but instead maintain stable spatial representations independently from grid cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed patterns of non-grid cell activity.

claim: On cued trials the spatial organisation of stopping behaviour and the proportion of hit trials was similar when grid activity was task-anchored versus task-independent.
source: On cued trials the spatial organisation of stopping behaviour (Figures 5C vs D and 6A) and the proportion of hit trials (Figure 6B) was similar for both groups.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figures 5C-D, 6A, and 6B.

claim: On non-beaconed and probe trials stopping behaviour was clearly spatial when grid activity was task-anchored, but spatial organisation was largely absent when grid activity was task-independent.
source: By contrast, on non-beaconed and probe trials stopping behaviour was clearly spatial when grid activity was task-anchored, but spatial organisation was largely absent when grid activity was task-independent (Figures 5C vs D and 6A), while the proportion of hit trials was substantially reduced (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figures 5C-D, 6A, and 6B.

claim: On non-beaconed and probe trials the proportion of hit trials was substantially reduced when grid activity was task-independent compared to task-anchored.
source: By contrast, on non-beaconed and probe trials stopping behaviour was clearly spatial when grid activity was task-anchored, but spatial organisation was largely absent when grid activity was task-independent (Figures 5C vs D and 6A), while the proportion of hit trials was substantially reduced (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: On trials when the reward zone cue was visible, adoption of the task-anchored representation did not predict task performance.
source: On trials when the reward zone cue was visible, adoption of the task-anchored representation did not predict task performance.
evidence: This is a summary of behavioral findings from the data.

claim: When the reward zone cue was absent, task-anchored grid firing was associated with successful localisation of the reward zone.
source: By contrast, when the reward zone cue was absent, task-anchored grid firing was associated with successful localisation of the reward zone.
evidence: This is a summary of behavioral findings from the data.

claim: Task-anchoring of the grid cell network selectively enhances performance of behaviours that require path integration.
source: Thus, our results suggest that task-anchoring of the grid cell network selectively enhances performance of behaviours that require path integration.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Grid representations support specific roles in path integration-dependent behaviours while arguing against the idea that grid codes provide a representation of location that is used more generally.
source: Our results support specific roles for task-anchored grid representations in path integration-dependent behaviours while arguing against the idea that grid codes provide a representation of location that is used more generally.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Grid representations can either be anchored to position in a task environment, or can provide an environment-independent distance metric.
source: Thus, we find that grid representations can either be anchored to position in a task environment, or can provide an environment-independent distance metric (Figure 2), that grid cells can switch between these operating modes within a behavioural session (Figures 3–4), and that anchoring of grid firing fields to location is not required for cued reward localisation, but appears to promote path integration-dependent reward localisation (Figures 5–6).
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Anchoring of grid firing fields to location is not required for cued reward localisation, but appears to promote path integration-dependent reward localisation.
source: Thus, we find that grid representations can either be anchored to position in a task environment, or can provide an environment-independent distance metric (Figure 2), that grid cells can switch between these operating modes within a behavioural session (Figures 3–4), and that anchoring of grid firing fields to location is not required for cued reward localisation, but appears to promote path integration-dependent reward localisation (Figures 5–6).
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figures 5-6.

claim: The MEC may implement multiple, parallel spatial computations.
source: By contrast, while some non-grid cells had activity that switched modes coherently with grid cells, many non-grid cells did not show task-independent periodic activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 5, Figures 4–5, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the MEC may implement multiple, parallel spatial computations.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed diversity of non-grid cell activity patterns.

claim: Grid representations are not necessarily anchored to the behaviourally relevant environmental reference frame.
source: In contrast, our results demonstrate that grid representations are not necessarily anchored to the behaviourally relevant environmental reference frame.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Both task-anchored and task-independent modes of grid representation can be observed during the same behavioural task.
source: Our results show that both modes of grid representation can be observed during the same behavioural task, and that the grid network can switch between these operating modes within a session.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: Simultaneously recorded grid cells switch modes coherently.
source: Consistent with the reported continuous attractor dynamics of grid networks, we find that simultaneously recorded grid cells switch modes coherently (Figures 4 and 5), although without recording from all grid cells simultaneously we cannot rule out the possibility that switching reflects a subset of grid cells that become disconnected from the wider network.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 4 and 5, with acknowledgment of a limitation.

claim: The mode switching observed differs from previously reported spontaneous remapping of MEC network states as the previously reported phenomenon was independent of any task contingencies and involved remapping between different task-anchored representations.
source: The mode switching we observe here appears to differ from previously reported spontaneous remapping of MEC network states (Low et al., 2021) as the previously reported phenomenon was independent of any task contingencies and involved remapping between different task-anchored representations.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work supported by citation.

claim: The switching observed in this study is between task-anchored representations that may be directly useful for solving the task at hand, and task-independent representations that appear unlikely to contribute to solving the task.
source: By contrast, we show here switching between task-anchored representations that may be directly useful for solving the task at hand, and task-independent representations that appear unlikely to contribute to solving the task.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings.

claim: A sub-population of non-grid cells appeared to switch between task-anchored and task-independent modes coherently with grid cells.
source: Among non-grid cells, a sub-population appeared to switch between task-anchored and task-independent modes coherently with grid cells.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from non-grid cell analysis.

claim: Task-independent periodic activity was relatively rare among non-grid cells.
source: However, task-independent periodic activity was relatively rare among non-grid cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The MEC might contain multiple sub-networks, with populations of grid cells and coherent non-grid cells sharing continuous attractor dynamics, while other populations of non-grid cells operate independently from the grid network.
source: A possible explanation for this dissociation is that the MEC might contain multiple sub-networks, with populations of grid cells and coherent non-grid cells sharing continuous attractor dynamics, while other populations of non-grid cells operate independently from the grid network.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed data patterns.

claim: Non-grid cells may be differentially influenced by visual cues.
source: For example, non-grid cells may be differentially influenced by visual cues (Casali et al., 2018; Kinkhabwala et al., 2020) or could generate location representations through ramping profiles rather than discrete firing fields (Tennant et al., 2022).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Non-grid cells could generate location representations through ramping profiles rather than discrete firing fields.
source: For example, non-grid cells may be differentially influenced by visual cues (Casali et al., 2018; Kinkhabwala et al., 2020) or could generate location representations through ramping profiles rather than discrete firing fields (Tennant et al., 2022).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The presence in the MEC of functionally distinct grid and non-grid networks might account for why manipulations that perturb grid cells selectively disrupt path integration-dependent behaviours.
source: The presence in the MEC of functionally distinct grid and non-grid networks might also account for why manipulations that perturb grid cells selectively disrupt path integration-dependent behaviours (Gil et al., 2018), whereas manipulations that target layer 2 stellate cells, which include grid and non-grid cells, impair path integration-dependent and cued behaviours (Qin et al., 2018; Tennant et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation connecting the current findings to prior experimental work.

claim: It appears unlikely that task-independent coding by grid cells result from failure of upstream circuits to generate appropriate visual representations.
source: It appears unlikely that task-independent coding by grid cells result from failure of upstream circuits to generate appropriate visual representations, e.g. through a shift in visual attention, as mice performed well on the visually cued version of the location memory task when grid cells were task-independent.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral performance data.

claim: Switching between firing modes may reflect modulatory pathways reducing the impact of visual inputs to the grid system, possibly reflecting top-down control mechanisms, shifts in brain state, or uncertainty about whether visual or motor signals indicate the correct environment.
source: A perhaps more promising hypothesis for future investigation is that switching reflects modulatory pathways reducing the impact of visual inputs to the grid system, possibly reflecting top-down control mechanisms, shifts in brain state, or uncertainty about whether visual or motor signals indicate the correct environment.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: Cued identification of a reward location is similar when grid cells are task-anchored or task-independent.
source: Our finding that cued identification of a reward location is similar when grid cells are task-anchored or task-independent suggests that grid representations are not required for cued recall of locations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the behavioral data.

claim: Grid representations are not required for cued recall of locations.
source: Our finding that cued identification of a reward location is similar when grid cells are task-anchored or task-independent suggests that grid representations are not required for cued recall of locations.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral findings.

claim: When both visual and grid inputs are available to downstream decision-making circuits, the grid input appears not to be used.
source: Thus, when both visual and grid inputs are available to downstream decision-making circuits, the grid input appears not to be used.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral data.

claim: If grid inputs were used when visual cues are available, then the inconsistent positional signals from the task-independent grid codes would impair performance.
source: If it was, then the inconsistent positional signals from the task-independent grid codes would impair performance.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be expected if grid codes were used.

claim: Cue-rich tracks often used to investigate grid activity patterns may not engage behaviours that require anchored grid firing.
source: An implication of this result is that cue-rich tracks often used to investigate grid activity patterns may not engage behaviours that require anchored grid firing.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings about the role of grid cells in cued tasks.

claim: Inactivation of stellate cells in layer 2 of the MEC causes deficits in the task used in this study and in other visually cued tasks.
source: First, inactivation of stellate cells in layer 2 of the MEC causes deficits in the task we use here and in other visually cued tasks (Qin et al., 2018; Tennant et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Other spatial tasks that involve selections between cued locations appear to require the MEC.
source: Second, other spatial tasks that involve selections between cued locations appear to require the MEC (e.g. Gaskin and White, 2013; Gaskin and White, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Spatial representations used for cued tasks could be encoded by other functional cell types, e.g. neurons that encode location through border or ramping firing fields, or through cue-responsive cells.
source: In this case, spatial representations used for the task could be encoded by other functional cell types, e.g. neurons that encode location through border (Solstad et al., 2008) or ramping firing fields (Tennant et al., 2022), or through cue-responsive cells (Casali et al., 2018; Keene et al., 2016; Kinkhabwala et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to prior work on other cell types.

claim: On trials in which the reward zone cue is absent, efficient reward localisation relies on path integration from the start of the track.
source: On trials in which the reward zone cue is absent, efficient reward localisation relies on path integration from the start of the track (Tennant et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: On trials without the reward zone cue, task-anchored grid firing was associated with a spatially localised stopping strategy and a higher proportion of successful trials compared with when grid firing was task-independent.
source: We found that on these trials, task-anchored grid firing was associated with a spatially localised stopping strategy and a higher proportion of successful trials compared with when grid firing was task-independent.
evidence: This is a summary of behavioral findings from the data.

claim: The findings corroborate key predictions of hypothesised roles for grid cells in path integration.
source: This corroborates key predictions of hypothesised roles for grid cells in path integration (McNaughton et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the findings to theoretical predictions.

claim: Explanations that behaviourally relevant computations are implemented elsewhere in the brain with grid anchoring to the track an indirect consequence are hard to reconcile with evidence that stellate cells in the MEC are required for the task.
source: It is conceivable that behaviourally relevant computations are implemented elsewhere in the brain with grid anchoring to the track an indirect consequence, but explanations of this kind are hard to reconcile with evidence that stellate cells in the MEC are required for the task we used here (Tennant et al., 2018), or with evidence for specific roles of grid firing in path integration based on genetic manipulations that abolish grid firing without affecting other functional cell types (Gil et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an argument against alternative explanations, supported by citations.

claim: Residual localisation performance on task-independent trials suggests that additional neural mechanisms may also support path integration-dependent behaviour.
source: Nevertheless, our finding of residual localisation performance on task-independent trials suggests that additional neural mechanisms may also support path integration-dependent behaviour.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of some successful performance without task-anchored grid firing.

claim: Residual localisation could reflect additional mechanisms for the implementation of path integration, e.g. through ramping activity.
source: This could reflect additional mechanisms for the implementation of path integration, e.g. through ramping activity (cf. Tennant et al., 2022).
evidence: This is speculation about alternative mechanisms, supported by a citation.

claim: Mice could in principle estimate track location with a system that utilises information about distance travelled obtained from task-independent grid representations.
source: Alternatively, mice could in principle estimate track location with a system that utilises information about distance travelled obtained from task-independent grid representations.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism.

claim: Because grid representations are available on the first entry to an environment they may be important for behaviour in newly experienced locations.
source: For example, because grid representations are available on the first entry to an environment they may be important for behaviour in newly experienced locations, whereas for familiar locations complementary representational strategies that emerge with learning may be sufficient.
evidence: This is speculation about when different mechanisms might be used.

claim: For familiar locations complementary representational strategies that emerge with learning may be sufficient.
source: For example, because grid representations are available on the first entry to an environment they may be important for behaviour in newly experienced locations, whereas for familiar locations complementary representational strategies that emerge with learning may be sufficient.
evidence: This is speculation about when different mechanisms might be used.

claim: Rather than being an 'always on' tracking system, grid cell networks vary in their engagement with the environment.
source: One implication of our results is that rather than being an 'always on' tracking system, grid cell networks vary in their engagement with the environment.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings about variable anchoring.

claim: Instability of grid anchoring may reflect control of the grid network by attentional or other top-down mechanisms.
source: This may reflect control of the grid network by attentional or other top-down mechanisms.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: Instability of grid anchoring could be an indirect consequence of mechanisms that control the structure and stability of place cell maps.
source: Alternatively, as the CA1 region of the hippocampus provides a major input to the MEC, instability of grid anchoring could be an indirect consequence of mechanisms that control the structure and stability of place cell maps (Krishnan et al., 2022; Pettit et al., 2022).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to prior work.

claim: An implication of the findings for investigations of grid cell activity using cue-rich environments is that in these experimental settings grid cells may not be influencing behavioural outcomes.
source: In either case, our results motivate a focus on grid cell activity in tasks that require path integration, while an implication of our finding for investigations of grid cell activity using cue-rich environments is that in these experimental settings grid cells may not be influencing behavioural outcomes.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings for experimental design.

claim: The results offer a new perspective on interindividual differences in path integration by humans.
source: Our results also offer a new perspective on interindividual differences in path integration by humans (e.g. Chrastil et al., 2017; Lakshminarasimhan et al., 2018; Petzschner and Glasauer, 2011).
evidence: This is speculation about broader implications, supported by citations.

claim: Rather than resulting from variation in path integration per se, differences between individuals could instead result from variation in the anchoring of grid representations underlying path integration.
source: Thus, rather than resulting from variation in path integration per se, differences between individuals could instead result from variation in the anchoring of grid representations underlying path integration.
evidence: This is speculation about mechanisms underlying individual differences.

claim: Variation in grid anchoring could be important as a potential mechanism for deficits in spatial localisation associated with neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: This could be important as a potential mechanism for deficits in spatial localisation associated with neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders (Kunz et al., 2015; Newton et al., 2023; Noel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation about clinical implications, supported by citations.

claim: Nine male C57BL/6J mice were used in this study.
source: Nine male C57BL/6J mice were used in this study.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental subjects.

claim: Three of the nine mice used in this study were also part of a previous study.
source: Three of the nine mice used here were also part of a previous study (Tennant et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental subjects.

claim: The virtual track had length 200 cm, with a 60 cm track zone, a 20 cm reward zone, a second 60 cm track zone, and a 60 cm black box to separate successive trials.
source: Virtual tracks, generated using Blender3D (blender.com) had length 200 cm, with a 60 cm track zone, a 20 cm reward zone, a second 60 cm track zone, and a 60 cm black box to separate successive trials.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental apparatus.

claim: The reward zone was either marked by distinct vertical green and black bars on 'beaconed' trials, or was not marked by a visual cue at all on 'non-beaconed' or 'probe' trials.
source: The reward zone was either marked by distinct vertical green and black bars on 'beaconed' trials, or was not marked by a visual cue at all on 'non-beaconed' or 'probe' trials.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental conditions.

claim: A stop was registered in Blender3D if the speed of the mouse dropped below 4.7 cm/s.
source: A stop was registered in Blender3D if the speed of the mouse dropped below 4.7 cm/s.
evidence: This is a direct description of the behavioral criterion.

claim: Trials were delivered in repeating blocks throughout a recording session.
source: Trials were delivered in repeating blocks throughout a recording session.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: The ratio and order of trial type delivery was not found to affect the results obtained.
source: The ratio and order of trial type delivery was not found to affect the results obtained (Figure 3—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claim: Units with firing rate >0.2 Hz, isolation >0.9, noise overlap <0.05, and peak signal-to-noise ratio >1 were used for further analysis.
source: Units with firing rate >0.2 Hz, isolation >0.9, noise overlap <0.05, and peak signal-to-noise ratio >1 were used for further analysis.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis criteria.

claim: Neurons were classified as grid cells when their grid score and spatial stability score was in the 99th percentile of the same scores from 1000 shuffled datasets.
source: Neurons were classified as grid cells when their grid score and spatial stability score was in the 99th percentile of the same scores from 1000 shuffled datasets.
evidence: This is a direct description of the classification method.
